query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: If a self-lubricating phase is induced in situ within the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix by incorporating a suitable precursor, then the alloy will maintain low friction and reduced wear across a sliding temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: A standard, single-phase CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy known to exhibit elevated friction and wear at higher temperatures.
generation.intervention: Incorporation of a precursor element or compound (without specifying its chemical class) into the CoCrFeNi alloy that, under sliding conditions and high temperature, transforms to form a lubricious, nanoscale second phase.
generation.conditions: Sliding experiments conducted over a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C, under varying loads and typical oxidizing environments encountered in service.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an in situ nanoscale tribofilm or dispersed lubricious phase at the sliding interface.
generation.mechanism: During sliding, the precursor reacts or transforms due to the combined effects of contact stress and thermal activation, generating a stable lubricious phase that forms a protective tribofilm. This film reduces friction and wear by providing a low-shear interface that is resilient over a broad temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified CoCrFeNi alloy will exhibit a significantly lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rates across the full temperature range compared to the unmodified baseline, as the self-generated lubricious phase continuously replenishes under operational conditions.
generation.baseline: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy lacking the precursor intervention, which shows high friction and wear at elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected to persist under moderate to high contact pressures and in oxidizing environments typical of high-temperature sliding, but may degrade under extreme mechanical loads or in highly aggressive chemical environments.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainties remain regarding the optimum nature and concentration of the precursor, the kinetics of the in situ phase transformation at various temperatures, and the long-term stability of the lubricious phase under cyclic loading.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi alloy samples: one with the precursor integrated to enable in situ self-lubrication and a control set without the precursor. Subject both sets to identical ball‐on‐disk tribological tests over a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C, under controlled load and environmental conditions.
measurements: Coefficient of friction (continuous monitoring during sliding)
Characterization of the sliding interface to detect the presence and continuity of the lubricious tribofilm (using SEM/TEM and spectroscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the intervention samples fail to demonstrate a statistically significant reduction (e.g., >20% lower) in both friction coefficient and wear rate compared to the control samples across most of the temperature range, or if no verifiable formation of the lubricious phase is detected at the sliding interface, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractHigh Entropy Alloys (HEAs) have garnered attention due to their remarkable tribological attributes. Predominantly, failure mechanisms in HEAs emanate from stress‐induced dislocations, culminating in crack propagation and film delamination. In this study, we report on the synthesis of 2D HEA of (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 which facilitates shear‐induced energy dissipation at sliding interfaces. The ball‐on‐disk tribological investigations demonstrate unprecedentedly low average coefficients of friction (0.076) and wear rates (10−9 mm3 (N∙m)−1) under high contact pressures (0.936 GPa) within ambient conditions. Employing multi‐scale characterizations alongside molecular dynamic simulations, we elucidate that the presence of the HEA triggers tribocatalytic activity under high contact pressures emerging as a pivotal factor in extending lubricant lifespan during tribological tests. The resilient lubriciousness coupled with the facile spray coating methodology of (MoWNbTaV)0.2S2 in ambient environments paves the way for the development of a new class of solid lubricants based on 2D HEA.
